summary: A concrete light on the tip of Ile Parisienne in Lake Superior's Whitefish Bay, built 1911-12, and the 1922 loss of the tender Lambton with the keepers bound for it.

lens.note: Second-order dioptric light in 1912 (Lake Carriers' Association, as LighthouseFriends prints it); current optic not described in the sources read

structures.type: hexagonal reinforced concrete tower with red lantern
structures.note: 58 ft from base to lantern vane (1912 description via LighthouseFriends); the Lighthouse Directory gives 9 m

staffing.note: The two keepers' houses are staffed in season as the first contact for eastbound vessels entering the Soo Traffic Control Area (Lighthouse Directory)

access.note: Accessible only by boat. Site and tower closed to visitors (Lighthouse Directory). The island's southeast 46 ha is privately owned.

events.note: Contract of 29 August 1911 with William Fryer of Collingwood for the tower, dwelling, oil shed, boathouse and wharf ($14,650); departmental inspector of work at the island September to November 1911
New lighthouse and fog signal commenced operations 15 September 1912 (Lake Carriers' Association, as LighthouseFriends prints it)
John Douglas hired as first keeper
Steamer Panther sank after a collision in fog with the steamer James J. Hill in Whitefish Bay; the Hill brought the Panther's crew to Sault Ste. Marie
CGS Lambton lost with all hands off Caribou Island on 19 April 1922, carrying keepers for the Lake Superior lights
Rest of the island became the Ile Parisienne Conservation Reserve

keepers.name: John Douglas
keepers.note: First keeper. LighthouseFriends says he was one of the keepers lost on the Lambton in April 1922; the departmental report names no keepers, so this is not confirmed.

wrecks.outcome: Sank after a fog collision with the steamer James J. Hill; crew taken to Sault Ste. Marie
wrecks.note: The paper's OCR reads 'Persian island' ('off Persian island In Whlteflsb bay'); the dispatch does not name Ile Parisienne, so the link is an inference (probably the same island, not confirmed). The report places the collision in Whitefish Bay per the dispatch; Wikipedia gives 26 June and 'James H. Hill' (not cited).

wrecks.outcome: Lost with all hands off Caribou Island in a severe storm, after leaving Sault Ste. Marie on 18 April with the lightkeepers aboard for the east end of Lake Superior
wrecks.note: Lighthouse Directory and the report give no keeper names; LighthouseFriends names the Ile Parisienne keeper and assistant as aboard; the 1922 AP wire names the Michipicoten and Caribou lights only

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The station record gives 1911 as the build year and the Lighthouse Directory gives 1912. The tower was contracted in August 1911 and worked on through that autumn; the light commenced operations on 15 September 1912 (LighthouseFriends, quoting the Lake Carriers' Association).

notes_for_editor: The Lambton: the departmental report (scan p. 112) and the 1922 AP wire (Milwaukee Leader, 26 April 1922) agree that the tender was lost with all hands in April 1922 off Caribou Island; the report does not name the keepers aboard and the AP wire gives 'about 17 men' against LighthouseFriends' five keepers and a crew of sixteen. The AP wire names only the Michipicoten and Caribou lights as the Lambton's errand; LighthouseFriends adds Ile Parisienne (keeper and assistant). The departmental printed page for the Lambton entry is unconfirmed (OCR head says p. 105?). John Douglas as one of the lost keepers is LighthouseFriends' claim only. The 1912-13 keepers' tables are OCR columns; no row for Ile Parisienne was matched by position, so the keepers John Douglas to C.N. McDonald rest on LighthouseFriends alone. Other Parisienne lines in the 1912-13 works tables (a 33-foot square wooden tower) could not be tied to this island by column and are not used. Panther: the newspaper's OCR reads the island as 'Persian'; the 1916 dateline is 28 June, Wikipedia gives 26 June and 'James H. Hill' (lead only; not cited). Heights: 58 ft (17.7 m) to the vane (LighthouseFriends), 16.6 m (station record), 9 m (Lighthouse Directory). Range: 12 miles (1912 description) against 9 nm (station record) and 25.75 km (Wikipedia lead); no range entered. Access: the Lighthouse Directory says site and tower closed; LighthouseFriends says grounds open. Staffing: the Lighthouse Directory says keepers' houses are staffed in season; the station record says unknown. Check before publishing: whether the seasonal staffing is current. Units: the 1912 description gives the visible range in miles (12 miles) and the story keeps that unit; no nautical-mile conversion was made. The Milwaukee Leader's dispatch is an undated Associated Press wire printed 26 April 1922; the story dates it to that paper's day only. The Panther dispatch is printed 5 July 1916 with a Sault Ste. Marie dateline of 28 June. FACT-CHECK 2026-10-27: every footnoted sentence was checked against the cached LighthouseFriends page, the Lighthouse Directory, the Canadian Register entry, the Marine report pages (Engineer's Branch travels p.53, Carson p.31, Lambton entry scan p.112, expenditure list p.55 confirmed) and both newspaper pages (Milwaukee Leader 26 April 1922 p.1; Vernon County Censor 5 July 1916 p.3, read through newspapers.py). Changes to the story: 'southern tip' became 'southwest end' (the 1912 description and the Directory both put the light at the southwest extremity or corner; 'southern tip' is the 1900s passage in LighthouseFriends). The tower height is now stated as disputed (58 ft / 17.7 m from the 1912 description, 9 m / 30 ft in the Directory). 'In a gale' changed to 'in a severe storm' (the report's words). The register's link to the Sault canal is worded as 'associated with', not as cause. 'Department's engineers' changed to 'the Department' (the report's travel passage does not say who). The 26 April 1922 date is the Milwaukee Leader's printing date; the wire itself is undated, and the story says so. The two counts of those aboard (AP: about 17 men; LighthouseFriends: sixteen crew and five keepers) are stated as disagreeing. The 1916 dispatch's 'Persian island' is kept as printed and flagged as not naming this island. OCR matched by position: 'He Parisienne' (the 1912 travels, p.53, and the 1913 Carson entry, p.31) reads 'He' for Ile in the OCR; the story reads it as Ile Parisienne. The 1913 works table lines 'Parisienne, ile' (scan p.59, printed p.52, a '33-foot high square wooden tower') could not be tied to this island and are not used. The Lambton entry's printed page is still unconfirmed (OCR head 'p.105?'; scan p.112); the footnote says so. The footnote's heading 'Dominion steamers' was not checked. Staffing ('staffed in season') is the Directory's current listing; check before publication.
